I had spent 2 days acting like both things were life or death, and it turned out there was a reasonable answer. The embarrassment is understandable. Can it also be information that your internal alarm is louder than the actual situation sometimes? I think so. I keep expecting people to be irritated when I need something, and then they are usually just practical. What did you do with the time that opened up? I finished the urgent case, left work before 7, and had dinner with Nora. Not a perfect evening. I checked my phone twice. But I did not open my laptop. How did Nora respond to the conversation you planned to have? Better than I expected. I told her that when I get stressed, I act like I want space, even when I actually need someone nearby. She said she can ask whether I want company or quiet instead of guessing. That sounds like a clear request from both of you. It felt vulnerable. I am used to trying to make my needs invisible, so nobody has to accommodate me. What is the cost of making them invisible? People cannot meet them. Then I feel lonely and resentful, even though I never told anyone what was happening. That is an important pattern to notice. How does it show up outside of work and home? With my sister. I decide what the other person probably has going on. Then I decide my need is not important enough to interrupt it. What information do you have when you make that decision? I said, She chose to be there It was not magic, but it stopped me from sending an apology text at midnight. That is a real shift. You let the connection stand without immediately trying to cancel it out. I think I do that at work too. Someone helps me and then I feel like I have to repay them right away. What happens when help is treated as a debt? I become less likely to ask for it, or I say yes to something I do not have capacity for because I feel I owe people. Is there a way to acknowledge help without turning it into a contract? I could just say thank you. I know that sounds obvious. Obvious and difficult can coexist. Keeping examples. I could make a small note on my phone, requests made, response received, what actually happened. items:
Anxiety and stress management:
- Continue practicing direct communication and setting boundaries at work and in personal relationships
- Continue monitoring for suicidal ideation and self-harm intent

- Discussed the difference between considering others and making decisions for them without allowing them to respond
- Explored the pattern of treating help as a debt and how it leads to overcommitment
- Discussed the concept of a "smaller reaching out practice" (e.g., texting sister to ask for a call without making it an emergency)
- Explored the difference between being considerate and making decisions for others
- Discussed the concept of a respectful request that gives the other person room to say yes, no, or not now
- Explored the pattern of feeling guilty after receiving help and how to acknowledge help without turning it into a contract
- Discussed the concept of collecting evidence that boundaries can be ordinary rather than catastrophic
- Patient to practice making direct requests at work and with sister
- Patient to take one lunch away from desk (15 minutes) with a coworker to practice connection
- Patient to keep a log of requests made, responses received, and actual outcomes to challenge catastrophic thinking
- Continue regular follow-up visits to monitor progress and safety
